item.title: Feeling Lost at Sea: Storytelling as a Tool for Resilience
item.description:
Resilience

Feeling Lost at Sea: Storytelling as a Tool for Resilience

How storytelling can navigate turbulent waters for deployed service members.

Posted August 16, 2026

Key points
  • Storytelling can foster connection, combat isolation, and build resilience in deployed service members.
  • Positive psychology programs have reduced suicides and improved well-being in the military.
  • Expressing personal stories through art, writing, or music can help reframe bleak realities.

In recent days, there has been extensive reporting on the mental health conditions of the sailors and Marines on the USS Abraham Lincoln, which has been deployed for a record-setting nine months (more than 260 days) off the coast of Iran. Additional reports highlight the physical conditions that include food quality and quantity, leading to morale issues that then circle back to mental health challenges where service members are reported to be trying to jump overboard, reportedly seeking suicide as an escape. I should also note that the Department of War and the Navy have pushed back on these claims, calling them isolated and otherwise without merit.

It’s fair to say the truth lies somewhere in between both perspectives, and as a well-being practitioner, I believe that even one suicide is one too many. I have never served in the military, no less spent an extended amount of time aboard a floating city, beyond a seven-day luxury cruise for a family vacation. Therefore, I cannot imagine the resiliency required to stay balanced on such an extended deployment where conditions are anything but luxury. That said, it’s important to explore, understand, and provide well-being tools as protective factors for these service members so that they can continue to find the mental fortitude to endure what is required of them as warriors and not resort to self-destructive behaviors that can spiral down toward the unrecoverable act of suicide.

History and Effectiveness of Military Resiliency Programs

Resiliency programs based in the science of positive psychology originally developed by Dr. Martin Seligman and colleagues at the University of Pennsylvania became institutionalized for the Army in 2008 as part of the Comprehensive Soldier Fitness program and later adopted in some version by other branches of the military, the Navy calling theirs the Operational Stress Control Program. These programs not only reduced suicides by extraordinary numbers, but they also increased the well-being of service members exponentially. This is the same program later brought to law enforcement by the FBI National Academy Associates that led to statewide programs in places like New Jersey that has trained every police officer in the state with the resiliency framework. Unfortunately, in June of 2025, the Department of War discontinued the Army’s Master Resiliency Trainer program, and service members will no longer be learning resiliency skills. However, to the best of my knowledge, the Navy program remains operational for now. These skills are known as positive psychology interventions and can support the well-being of service members, especially when faced with adversities like those being reported on one of the largest, most capable aircraft carriers in the world.

One of the most basic positive interventions known in the space is the idea of giving and receiving gratitude. It’s free, takes little effort, and has the most positive results toward subjective well-being. This seems like an easy “fix,” and as Holocaust survivor Viktor Frankl has previously explained, even in the worst of conditions we can always find something to be grateful for. However, I fear the conditions on the ship may be so dire that a suggestion to be more grateful could present as insensitive and not well-received. So, what type of intervention honors the reality and provides a life preserver for these sailors and Marines so that even in despair, they can work toward optimism and not consider suicide as an option?

The Power of Storytelling as a Well-Being Intervention

I believe the power of storytelling can be an answer. Storytelling is an evidence-based intervention that supports healing and what Aristotle identified as living well, known as eudaimonia—literally translated into Good Spirit. The act of telling a story can be done in a variety of ways that allows the storyteller and listener to find a medium that best connects with the individual. From the spoken to written word and physical art to music, there are a variety of ways to connect with story in either an immersive or expressive way. Stories support connection while reducing isolation and loneliness. A story can assign meaning and purpose when we seem to have lost the use of our personal rudder. It can drive us to engagement and recalibrate our compass when we feel lost at sea. And finally, the power of storytelling can help us feel positive emotions when we highlight our accomplishments and apply our contributions through the lens of the best version of ourselves.

So as this conflict with Iran requires unprecedented commitment by the sailors and Marines in the region, I would respectfully suggest to leadership at all levels that these men and women be given the instruction and supplies to find ways that they can tell their stories and overtly express themselves. Doing so can allow them to recognize their reality and reframe their experiences where they can live on paper through words, in color through art, or in the creativity of music so that their thoughts and emotions do not ruminate solely between their ears and cloud their personal and professional judgment. Storytelling supports resiliency and a resilient staff is a productive and willing workforce aligned with purpose. Individuals with purpose are optimistic, and optimism is a protective factor against self-destructive behavior including suicidal ideation. The power of storytelling is real and is certain to change the tides affecting those at sea.

If you or someone you love is contemplating suicide, seek help immediately. For help 24/7 dial 988 for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or reach out to the Crisis Text Line by texting TALK to 741741. To find a therapist, please visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: AI and Subtractive Innovation
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI and Subtractive Innovation

When AI makes thinking less necessary.

Posted August 16, 2026

Key points
  • AI can make us more capable while asking us to think less.
  • The real shift may begin when thinking simply isn't necessary anymore.
  • What happens when the easier choice is to let the machine do it?
Source: VIVIANE M./Pixabay

Three years ago, I wrote a post asking whether artificial intelligence might eventually place human cognition on the technological chopping block. At that time, AI was beginning to reveal what it could do, and the concern seemed fairly straightforward. Innovation has always created obsolescence. Machines replaced physical labor, calculators took over much of routine arithmetic, and digital technologies displaced entire industries. But now the domain of innovation is less about that old stereo or calculator but human thought itself.

OK, cognition hasn't become obsolete per se. In fact, AI has made us astonishingly more capable. Scientists can explore hypotheses faster, physicians can interrogate complex medical information, and you and I can analyze, write, code, or create at levels that previously required specialized (and expensive) expertise. It's truly remarkable and I don't think we should diminish it simply because we're concerned about some of the consequences.

I've called one expression of this Iterative Intelligence—the back-and-forth between human and machine in which an idea gets questioned, reframed, and sometimes pushed somewhere neither would have taken it alone. And while this is new, it also harkens back to the venerable Socratic dialogue. Used in this context, the technology doesn't necessarily reduce thinking. Sometimes it creates more of it. So I'm increasingly uncomfortable with the simple question of whether AI is making us smarter or dumber. Something more complicated may be happening.

Obsolescence Begins With Necessity

We tend to think of obsolescence as an endpoint. Something works until a better technology arrives and eventually the old thing gets thrown away. Film cameras, fax machines, and typewriters come to mind. But before any of them disappeared, something more consequential happens and this is important to recognize. We simply stopped needing them. And perhaps that's a better way to think about cognition in the context of AI.

AI doesn't have to destroy my ability to write. It only has to make writing something myself less necessary. My memory doesn't have to deteriorate if remembering becomes less important. And my ability to construct an argument doesn't have to disappear if a reasonable argument can be generated before I've even worked through it.

This leads me to a concept I think of as Subtractive Innovation. That's when innovation increases the capability of the human-machine system while reducing the necessity for the human to exercise the capability being augmented. And I think the word necessity is critical here as I'm not arguing that using AI inevitably makes us cognitively weaker. Human beings have been offloading cognitive tasks onto tools for thousands of years, and many of those tools have made us smarter and more capable. AI may do the same on a scale we have never seen before.

So, here's what concerns me. Human abilities tend to have a "use-it-or-lose-it" quality. When we don't need to do something, we generally do it less. And if we do it less, I think it's reasonable to wonder what happens to the underlying capability over time. I don't think we know the answer yet, but the pathway is certainly worth paying attention to.

When Thinking Becomes Optional

A blank page once required someone to write the first sentence. An argument had to be constructed, and even asking a good question usually required enough understanding to know what you didn't know.

So, here's the point: Increasingly, these things are optional.

AI can start the page, finish it, and summarize it. And here's where it gets interesting: Every one of those choices can be completely rational. Why spend 20 minutes doing something that can be accomplished in 20 seconds, particularly when the result may be just as good or even better?

This is where I'd suggest that Subtractive Innovation becomes different from simple cognitive offloading. AI isn't taking our ability to think away from us. It's removing, piece by piece and thought by thought, some of the necessity to think for ourselves. Cognitive surrender, if it happens, probably won't come from some dramatic decision to turn our minds over to machines. It may emerge almost unnoticed through thousands of sensible decisions to avoid effort that technology has made unnecessary.

The Choice Inside the Machine

Iterative Intelligence offers another path. Instead of asking AI to eliminate the cognitive act, we can use it to extend that act. We can challenge its answer, change the premise, find the contradiction, or follow an association we hadn't considered. Two people can use exactly the same AI and arrive at equally impressive outputs while having very different cognitive experiences. One may have used the machine primarily to complete the task, while the other used it to change the thought. Curiously, this path isn't the shortest distance from question to answer, it's the longer and bumpy experiential path of discovery and learning.

This brings me to the idea of abundance, another word that has become almost inseparable from the promise of AI. I've written before about the strange dynamics of cognitive abundance, and I think Subtractive Innovation adds another dimension to it. We tend to assume the math moves in one direction—more intelligence available to us should mean more intelligence for us.

I'm not sure the equation is that simple.

The abundance of machine capability can make the human-machine system dramatically more powerful while simultaneously making some human capabilities less necessary. Both things can be true at once. We can have more intelligence available to us and fewer reasons to exercise our own.

A technological lifetime ago, about three years, I wondered if cognition itself might eventually become obsolete. Today, I think obsolescence may be the wrong place to begin looking. The earlier signal is necessity. A capability can remain perfectly intact while becoming progressively less necessary, and perhaps that's where the real cognitive consequences begin.

AI may indeed usher in an age of abundance. But the math may not move in only one direction. And more at the level of the system doesn't necessarily mean more at the level of the human.

And that leaves me with a slightly different question. What happens to humans when thinking becomes optional?

item.title: The Tower of Babel, Tyranny, and AI
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

The Tower of Babel, Tyranny, and AI

Amassing information often precedes the centralization of power.

Posted August 16, 2026

Key points
  • The Tower of Babel story addresses the desire of some human beings to dominate others.
  • The amassing of information often precedes the imposition of tyranny.
  • AI provides unprecedented opportunities to centralize information.

In the Book of Genesis Tower of Babel story, members of a united human race, all speaking the same language, come to a land in the east where they decide to build for themselves a tower that will reach all the way up into the heavens, enabling them to “make a name for themselves.” God, recognizing this as but the beginning of what such a united, monoglot humanity would do, decides to scatter them all over the earth and render them incapable of understanding one another. The place is called Babel, because the speech of each proved to be incomprehensible to the others, like mere babbling.

Tower of Babel, Pieter Bruegel the Elder (1563).
Source: Wikimedia Commons/Public Domain

The most common interpretation treats Babel as an origin myth, intended to explain why the different peoples of the earth speak different languages. In another common view, it represents an indictment of pride, the notion that human beings could become self-sufficient and cast off all use for God. A third view regards it as an even greater rebellion, a human effort to transform human beings into divinities and thereby completely supplant the divine. A fourth finds in it a reminder that the encounter between the human and God cannot be engineered by humans and always depends utterly on divine action.

Relevance of the Babel Story in the Age of Surveillance Technology

Yet there is another interpretation that deserves special attention in our own day, when new technologies are making it possible for authorities to monitor the location, movements, purchases, plans, private conversations, and even thoughts of individuals to a far greater extent than ever before. Cities are peppered with cameras that track license plates and recognize faces; the universal adoption of cellphones provides ready access to nearly everyone’s data and voice transmissions; new technologies can even monitor heart rate, body temperature, and brain waves, providing insight into who might be nervous or lying.

How will the world’s dictators and would-be autocrats respond to such capabilities? Will they scrupulously eschew them, out of a deep and abiding dedication to protecting and preserving their citizens’ political liberties? Or will they take whatever steps necessary to install and exploit such surveillance technologies to their full potential, in order to amass and wield power? Suppose, for example, that all the information that cellphones are capable of harvesting could be collected, collated, and analyzed by AI, providing on-demand detailed reports about each person’s activities.

The Babel story’s use of phrases such as “one language” and “same words” may have more than a merely linguistic connotation. Perhaps it is referring to an ideology. Consider Leninism, which in the early years of the Soviet Union sought to create a one-party state, ban factions, and introduce the red terror. In order to create a more perfect union, Lenin argued, opposing points of view needed to be repressed and political rivals needed to be imprisoned or executed. No threats to Bolshevik power were to be tolerated.

Babel as a Warning Against Ideological and Political Monopolies

The Hebrew Scriptures are full of warnings about the dangers of autocracy, expressed in the texts as kingship. By the time of the prophet Samuel, the people of Israel had lived free of the rule of an earthly king since they fled Pharaoh’s rule in Egypt. Yet the people cried out for such a ruler, someone around whom their sense of national identity could coalesce and who could lead them in battle. All their neighbors had kings, and they wanted one, too. In short, the covenant with God was not enough. Yet Samuel warned them that kings would be selfish and sinful, exploiting their labor and imposing heavy taxes. The largely unchecked power of kings would only magnify and perpetuate the worst human tendencies.

The Tower of Babel story may be read as a warning against autocracy and ideology. Perhaps it was not all people but only some people, those who coveted power over others, who wanted to build a tower, and perhaps they saw this project as a means of uniting people under a single ideology. Rather than allow people to scatter over the earth, each family and village tending to itself, they wanted to bind everyone to their own purpose. The tower, a symbol of this unification, would raise not all men but only those who sat at the top, commanding everyone else. It would be a monument not to humankind but to the power of a handful of men, elevating but a crafty few.

God, seeing the people united around this one language, this one ideology, sees that building the tower is but the first step in the rulers’ exploitation of the people. So long as the people know only one ideology, one way of understanding, assessing, and acting in the world, they will be fodder for tyranny. What they need are other languages, other accounts, other ways of finding meaning in life. What matters most is not legitimizing a dominant political order but living in accordance with a higher, divine order, one that instead of shoehorning all thought and communication into the same system tolerates and even celebrates diverse points of view.
